messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol Alvarez was 44 when she sought treatment, a married radiologist who had spent years in hospital reading rooms built around dim light, humming machines, and long stretches of vigilance. The assault happened after an evening shift, when she left through a side staff entrance she had used countless times before. A man forced her into a secluded area of the parking structure and raped her. What remained with her most vividly was not only the physical violation but the moment she realized how quickly ordinary cues had become dangerous: the echo of footsteps behind her, the glimpse of a face she had not properly registered, the sickening awareness that she had not been able to stop what was happening. In the days afterward, she could not shake the sense that the world had changed from predictable to predatory.

Over the following months, Marisol moved through her life as if danger were always about to step into view. She found herself scanning faces with unusual intensity, studying the set of a jaw, the angle of a body in a hallway, the way a stranger held himself near an elevator. In the hospital she began positioning herself carefully in conference rooms and cafeterias, choosing chairs with her back against the wall so she could see the door and the whole room at once. Even at home, sitting with her husband in their kitchen, she noticed she was unable to settle into the chair if the room was behind her. She understood, intellectually, that she was often in safe places; her body did not accept that conclusion. She stayed braced, shoulders tight, eyes moving, as if missing one detail might leave her exposed again.

That constant alertness shaped how she came to think about herself. Each time she caught herself silently assessing a colleague’s expression for menace, or felt her chest tighten until she had moved to a seat facing the entrance, it seemed to confirm something bleak in her mind. She had come to believe that her reactions proved she was a lousy coper, someone who should have been able to put the event behind her but had instead become ruled by it. The fact that she could not relax even in places she knew were secure deepened her conviction that something in her had been permanently altered for the worse. More than once she thought, with shame and certainty, that if she were stronger, smarter, or less damaged, she would not still be living like this.

The same watchfulness also fed a harsher sense of helplessness. Because she was continually searching faces and body language for signs of threat, the world appeared crowded with possible danger. A stranger’s neutral glance in the parking lot, a technician stepping too close in a cramped corridor, a man lingering near the elevators at the end of the day—each could hold her attention for hours afterward. Living this way made her feel that bad things could happen at any moment and that she could not stop them. She was certain now that safety depended on never letting her guard down, and that belief left her feeling both responsible for preventing another assault and fundamentally unable to guarantee that she could.

At work, the consequences had become difficult to hide. Radiology had always suited her precision, but now her need to monitor the environment intruded on the concentration her job required. In multidisciplinary meetings she arrived early to secure a seat against the wall, and if that spot was taken she spent much of the discussion tense and half-absorbed, tracking who entered and where they stood. She lingered after shifts until other staff were leaving so she would not walk to the garage alone, and she scrutinized security guards and hospital employees with the same guarded attention she gave strangers. These habits made sense to her; they were how she kept from being caught off guard again. Yet the more she lived in this narrowed, defended way, the more she saw herself as diminished—less capable, less resilient, no longer the steady physician she had once trusted herself to be.

Her husband had begun to notice that she rarely seemed at ease. Even on quiet evenings, she sat upright, listening, preferring the corner seat in restaurants and scanning nearby tables before she could join a conversation. Marisol did not describe this as fear so much as necessity. What frightened her most was the idea that this was now her permanent condition: a woman who could read a CT scan with calm authority but could not sit in a safe room without planning exits and assessing faces. She finally came for help after realizing that she was arranging nearly every part of her day around vigilance and that this very pattern had become evidence, in her own mind, that the assault had changed her irrevocably. She wanted relief, but she was afraid the stronger truth was that she was no longer capable of feeling safe, and that the life she had before was not recoverable.
